title: The winds that scatter
hookLine: by the winds that scatter, and the clouds that carry (51:1–2)

lines: BLOCK D: TOWARDS THE THIRTIETH PART.
cards: Block D: towards the thirtieth part. Over the next ten weeks or so, the path walks from Surah Adh-Dhariyat, the fifty-first, toward the short surahs that close the book.
The surahs get shorter and the sound changes: quicker lines, oaths piling up one after another.
And the very first thing this block does is swear by something you can't see, only feel on your face: the wind, the thing that scatters.

teach.b: Surah Adh-Dhariyat opens with four oaths, each a short line in Arabic.

teach.h: WINNOWING: WIND THAT LIFTS AND SCATTERS.
teach.b: Pickthall's translation of the first two: "By those that winnow with a winnowing, And those that bear the burden (of the rain)." Winnowing is an old farm picture: tossing grain in the air so the wind blows the chaff away.
Adh-dhariyat are the scatterers, the winds that lift dust and seed and carry them off. Then al-hamilat, the carriers, bearing a heavy load: the clouds, full of rain.
Then al-jariyat, those that run easily, and al-muqassimat, those that distribute by command. The verse doesn't say who these are; it gives only what they do. So people asked.
A report preserved by the commentators says 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, preaching in Kufa, invited questions, and someone asked about these opening words.
He answered: the scatterers are the winds, the carriers are the clouds, the runners are the ships, and the distributors are the angels. Notice the movement. Wind lifts water to the sky.
Cloud carries it. Ships run on the water the wind pushes. And angels distribute, by command, the provision all of it brings.

teach.h: WEATHER AS A CHAIN OF DELIVERY.
teach.b: Read that way, ordinary weather becomes a chain of delivery. Why open with an oath? In the Qur'an an oath draws attention: look at this, then hear what follows.
The next verses answer: what you are promised is true, and the judgment will come. The surah swears by ordinary things in motion to make a claim about something no one can yet see.

how: When strong wind blows, Muslims have a supplication taught in hadith that asks for its good and seeks refuge from its harm.

o: the scattering winds that lift and carry
the angels who record a person's deeds
the stars that guide travelers at night

games.q: four oaths, by 'Ali's reading — tap the pairs.

s: the verses name the winds, clouds, ships and angels directly
they give only what each does; 'Ali's explanation names them.
Block D moves toward the short surahs at the end of the book
towards the thirtieth part, the last juz'.
winnowing means tossing grain so the wind takes the chaff
it's the farm picture behind adh-dhariyat.

games.q: someone in Kufa asks 'Ali what 'those that winnow' are. what does he say?
games.why: winds, then clouds, ships and angels: a chain of delivery from sky to provision.

practice: If you can, step outside or open a window; if not, remember the last wind you felt. Notice where it touches, your face, your hands, the back of your neck, and watch for something it moves: a leaf, a curtain, your hair.
You only know it by what it moves, and if you pray, you can say subhanallah, glory to Allah, with each gust.

wordCard.voice: Adh-dhariyat: the winnowing winds of 51:1, which 'Ali read as the first link in a chain of winds, clouds, ships and angels. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: the scatterers, the winnowing winds; the word that names surah 51.

carryVoice: Your line: by the scattering winds. The unseen is known by what it moves. See you tomorrow.
